results.name: round_number_target_bonus
results.description: Among sets with no example ending in 0, yes-rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus non-example targets within 1-2 of a multiple of 10; observed > null means people favour round numbers as program outputs, which the model (final-digit similarity only to shown examples) under-produces.
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bonus
# description: Among sets with no example ending in 0, yes-rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus non-example targets within 1-2 of a multiple of 10; observed > null means people favour round numbers as program outputs, which the model (final-digit similarity only to shown examples) under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    no_zero = ~np.any(np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=1.0) % 10 == 0, axis=1)
    r = t % 10
    m = no_zero & ~is_ex
    return rate(m & (r == 0)) - rate(m & ((r == 1) | (r == 2) | (r == 8) | (r == 9)))

results.name: tiny_target_rejection
results.description: Among sets whose smallest example is >= 15, yes-rate for targets 1-3 minus targets 4-10; observed < null means people reject the very smallest numbers (1, 2, 3) more than graded size similarity predicts (model over-produces yes on them).

# description: Among sets whose smallest example is >= 15, yes-rate for targets 1-3 minus targets 4-10; observed < null means people reject the very smallest numbers (1, 2, 3) more than graded size similarity predicts (model over-produces yes on them).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)

results.name: wide_span_fill_in
results.description: Yes-rate on in-span non-example targets for sets whose span (max-min) is >= 50 minus sets whose span is <= 25 (k >= 2); observed < null means people do not fill in wide spans the way the model's zero size mismatch inside the span predicts (model over-produces yes in wide spans), observed > null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: wide_span_fill_in
# description: Yes-rate on in-span non-example targets for sets whose span (max-min) is >= 50 minus sets whose span is <= 25 (k >= 2); observed < null means people do not fill in wide spans the way the model's zero size mismatch inside the span predicts (model over-produces yes in wide spans), observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    inspan = (t > mn) & (t < mx) & ~is_ex & (k >= 2)
    span = mx - mn
    return rate(inspan & (span >= 50)) - rate(inspan & (span <= 25))

results.name: inspan_below_start_overreach
results.description: In sets that go up overall (last > first) where the first example is not the smallest, yes-rate on in-span non-example targets below the first example minus in-span non-example targets above it; observed > null means the model over-penalizes in-span numbers below the 'start' (people only reject numbers below the smallest example, not below the first one).
results.code:
# name: inspan_below_start_overreach
# description: In sets that go up overall (last > first) where the first example is not the smallest, yes-rate on in-span non-example targets below the first example minus in-span non-example targets above it; observed > null means the model over-penalizes in-span numbers below the 'start' (people only reject numbers below the smallest example, not below the first one).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    inspan = (t > mn) & (t < mx) & ~is_ex & (last > first) & (first > mn)
    return rate(inspan & (t < first)) - rate(inspan & (t > first))

results.name: far_generalization_by_set_size
results.description: Yes-rate on out-of-span non-example targets at least 20 from the nearest span edge for 3-4-example sets minus 1-2-example sets; observed < null means more examples narrow far generalization more than the model produces (size principle under-produced), observed > null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: far_generalization_by_set_size
# description: Yes-rate on out-of-span non-example targets at least 20 from the nearest span edge for 3-4-example sets minus 1-2-example sets; observed < null means more examples narrow far generalization more than the model produces (size principle under-produced), observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    gap = np.maximum(mn - t, t - mx)
    far = (gap >= 20) & ~is_ex
    return rate(far & (k >= 3)) - rate(far & (k <= 2))

results.name: example_primacy_vs_recency
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate when the target equals the first shown example minus when it equals the last shown example; observed > null means people endorse earlier examples as much as or more than later ones, i.e. the model's recency weighting over-favours the last example (and vice versa).
results.code:
# name: example_primacy_vs_recency
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate when the target equals the first shown example minus when it equals the last shown example; observed > null means people endorse earlier examples as much as or more than later ones, i.e. the model's recency weighting over-favours the last example (and vice versa).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    m = k >= 2
    return rate(m & (t == first)) - rate(m & (t == last))

results.name: descending_downward_generalization
results.description: In sets that go down overall (last < first), yes-rate for targets 1-30 below the smallest example minus targets 1-30 above the largest; observed < null means people generalize downward less than upward even with no upward starting point (the model, lacking a start penalty and with momentum favouring the travel direction, over-produces downward yeses here).
results.code:
# name: descending_downward_generalization
# description: In sets that go down overall (last < first), yes-rate for targets 1-30 below the smallest example minus targets 1-30 above the largest; observed < null means people generalize downward less than upward even with no upward starting point (the model, lacking a start penalty and with momentum favouring the travel direction, over-produces downward yeses here).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    desc = last < first
    return rate(desc & (mn - t >= 1) & (mn - t <= 30)) - rate(desc & (t - mx >= 1) & (t - mx <= 30))

results.name: edge_step_sharpness
results.description: Among out-of-span non-example targets, yes-rate at gap 1-5 from the nearest span edge minus yes-rate at gap 6-15; observed > null means generalization drops off more sharply just past the span edge than the model's smooth exponential size similarity produces, observed < null means a flatter fall-off.
results.code:
# name: edge_step_sharpness
# description: Among out-of-span non-example targets, yes-rate at gap 1-5 from the nearest span edge minus yes-rate at gap 6-15; observed > null means generalization drops off more sharply just past the span edge than the model's smooth exponential size similarity produces, observed < null means a flatter fall-off.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    first = ex[:, 0]
    last = ex[np.arange(len(ex)), k - 1]
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    gap = np.maximum(mn - t, t - mx)
    m = ~is_ex & (gap >= 1)
    return rate(m & (gap <= 5)) - rate(m & (gap >= 6) & (gap <= 15))
